title: Canada’s climate record criticized as UN talks end with impasse on fossil fuels
html:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, right, and United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell attend the official close of the conference in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.Kaan Soyturk/Reuters

United Nations climate talks ended Sunday without reaching an overarching agreement on disputes about whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had been low heading into the two-week negotiations in Turkey at the 31st annual meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, or COP31.

That’s despite continuous news of calamitous climate events, including heat waves in Europe, forest fires in North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal that has killed at least 1,500 people. October witnessed the largest temperature increase above preindustrial temperatures of any month on record at 1.8 degrees Celsius, according to Berkeley Earth.

Impasses over explicitly including fossil fuels and other issues, including money, proved irreconcilable. Negotiators, activists and even organizers used the word “disappointing” to characterize the discussions.

“It was depressing and a bit of a roller-coaster ride, because for the first time we had a COP where the conversation about fossil fuel phaseout was front and centre,” including 80-plus meetings on the topic, attendee Tzeporah Berman, Vancouver-based chair of the global Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told The Globe and Mail.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” adding that “every delay makes our task harder and more costly” to counter climate change.

A UN body this year said it is inevitable that the world will surpass the warming threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which countries pledged to limit long-term warming to 1.5 degrees above preindustrial times.

Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said on X Sunday: “While the outcome of COP31 was not what we hoped, Canada’s commitment to the Paris Agreement, multilateralism and international institutions remains steadfast. We’ll continue active dialogue with all willing partners to ensure that the UNFCCC process works.”

Former federal environment minister Catherine McKenna, chair of the UN Secretary-General’s High-Level Expert Group on Net-Zero, told The Globe that “it’s always better to have no deal than a bad deal, and having an agreement that doesn’t include fossil fuels, which are driving the climate crisis, would be bonkers.”

The two-week meeting, which ended Sunday in the resort town of Antalya, did make progress on smaller issues. Nearly 100 signed onto a proposal introduced separately from the main agreement calling for countries to increase the share of electricity in total final energy consumption from about 21 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.

Canada made several modest funding announcements, including up to $10-million for a climate, risk and early warning systems initiative. It also signed a memorandum of understanding with British International Investment and Norfund to strengthen collaboration on climate and energy transition investments in emerging markets.

But Prime Minister Mark Carney and other world leaders were tagged “fossil of the day” by Climate Action Network International for not attending COP31. That’s the latest in a growing stream of criticism toward the federal government over its seemingly lacklustre commitment to the climate file.

One-time environment minister and ex-Greenpeace activist Steven Guilbeault quit Mr. Carney’s cabinet last fall after Ottawa signed a memorandum of understanding with Alberta to jointly explore a new pipeline to the Pacific coast. He later resigned as an MP, saying the government was “backsliding” on action to counter climate change.

In September, the Canadian Climate Institute said the country is more than 20 years behind reaching its 2030 emissions target and that its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 will be unreachable without significant policy improvements.

Turkey’s Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, left, Canada’s Minister of Environment, Climate Change and Nature Julie Dabrusin, middle, and Ian L. Edwards, president and CEO of AtkinsRealis, attend an event at COP31.Kaan Soyturk/Reuters

Despite Ms. Dabrusin’s attendance at COP31, “Overall, Canada was missing in action at the climate talks,” said Ms. Berman, who criticized efforts by the Carney government to expand production and exports of fossil fuels. “How do you phase something out by building more of it?”

Canadian Katherine Hayhoe, chief scientist with the global non-profit The Nature Conservancy, told The Globe that, 11 years after the Paris deal, “we’re starting to see the separation between the countries who really mean it and the countries that don’t.” Asked which category applied to Canada, she said, “That is a question I would really like the answer to.”

Ms. McKenna, who is also chief executive of Ottawa-based advisory firm Climate and Nature Solutions, said “Canada is so far away from what it committed to” in Paris. “It’s not just about showing up, it’s actually about doing the work.”

She said overreliance on fossil fuels “is a huge risk” as other countries invest in renewable and clean energy in a more pronounced way. “It’s not just recognizing that Canada has an obligation” under the Paris Agreement, “it’s also about taking advantage of the economic opportunity of the clean energy transition and not getting stuck with stranded assets.”

Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership, which didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A much larger number of countries accepted the decision, often reluctantly, saying consensus on something was more important, though it ultimately failed. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

Earlier in the week, Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and needed to be reformed.

Caroline Brouillette, executive director of Climate Action Network Canada, said in a statement “what happened at COP31 is a symptom of a decaying process, which has become increasingly disconnected from the state of the world.”

Despite COP31’s failure, there were signs of progress in other forums. The Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative said it now has high-level government support from 30 countries, including Panama, Kenya, Ghana and Guatemala, and several island nations, including Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu - but not Canada.

They met in Turkey to advance plans to phase out fossil fuels. Ireland and Tuvalu, meanwhile, announced they would co-host the next meeting of a separate fossil fuel phaseout initiative, known as the Santa Marta Process.

“What was exciting in Turkey is that there are now clearly three diplomatic tracks on climate negotiations, with the emergence of new outside processes that are not being held hostage by the oil and gas lobby” or limited by COP’s consensus structure, said Ms. Berman. They “could help create a breakthrough on an issue that was stuck within the existing climate negotiations.”

Fossil fuels went unmentioned in COP final decisions for more than 25 years, said Alden Meyer, with the think tank E3G. At the COP meeting in 2023, in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, the concluding agreement called for the first time for “transitioning away from fossil fuels.” The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai agreement, but that wasn’t enough for many countries or environmental groups.

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many countries and activists said would undermine efforts to reduce overall emissions. Other climate issues weren’t settled. many were deferred to next year’s meeting in Ethiopia.

Manuel Pulgar-Vidal, president of COP20 and now climate energy lead at the World Wildlife Fund, said “COP31 left too much undone.

“The climate will not wait for governments to find their courage.”

With reports from The Associated Press
summary: Although the COP31 outcome was not as hoped, Canada remains committed to the Paris Agreement, Environment Minister says
